vignette:
He is 49, a European man who has spent most of his adult life learning how to stay composed in public. As a city council member, he is known for measured language, long meetings, and the ability to sit through conflict without showing much strain. People describe him as steady. His wife says that is true only in certain rooms.

He joins the military in his early twenties, before marriage, before local politics, before he becomes the kind of man who keeps three calendars and remembers every committee deadline. He rarely speaks about why he enlisted. When he does, he makes it sound practical: work, structure, service. During deployment, his unit is caught in an ambush on a road they have traveled many times. He remembers the ordinary details with painful clarity: the heat inside the vehicle, the stale smell of gear, someone complaining about bad coffee. Then the explosion. He does not tell it dramatically. He says there is first a bright flash and then a strange flattening of sound, as if the world has been packed with cotton. He sees one of the men beside him slumped at an angle that makes no sense. He feels himself moving before he is fully aware, dragging, shouting, scanning, firing. Training takes over where thought cannot.

What stays with him is not only terror but the conviction, formed in seconds and never fully shaken, that life can split open without warning. Afterward, he returns home with no visible injury. People congratulate him, buy him drinks, ask broad questions he can answer with easy phrases. He discovers quickly which version of the story others can tolerate. He offers that version often enough that it becomes polished, almost detached from what he actually remembers at night.

He marries, starts a family, and moves into public service by degrees. He likes local government because it feels concrete: roads repaired, budgets balanced, parks opened, grievances heard. He tells himself that if he can keep order in small civic ways, he is doing something decent. Yet the habits from combat settle into daily life instead of fading. In restaurants, he chooses the seat facing the door. At public forums, he scans the room before he hears the first speaker. When a motorcycle backfires outside council chambers, his shoulders tense before he can think. Once, during a veterans' event in the town square, a ceremonial salute sends his heart pounding so hard he has to grip the podium and pause as if searching for notes.

At home, the cost is clearer. He sleeps lightly and often wakes drenched in sweat, already on edge, his wife startled beside him. Sometimes he jerks awake convinced he has heard shouting or metal tearing. He checks locks, windows, the driveway. On those nights he cannot return to bed, so he sits in the kitchen in the dark, scrolling through local news and telling himself he is just getting an early start. His wife has learned that touching him unexpectedly when he is asleep can make him lash out with a frightened, defensive shove, after which he is flooded with shame. He apologizes repeatedly, then withdraws.

He avoids war films, Remembrance Day broadcasts, and certain smells that pull him backward instantly-diesel, hot rubber, wet canvas. He insists he is not avoiding anything, only "not interested." But he takes long detours to avoid the military cemetery where a former comrade is buried. He has never visited the grave. The thought of standing there feels unbearable, as if it would collapse the distance he has spent years building.

In council meetings, colleagues notice he can become disproportionately sharp when discussions turn chaotic. A minor procedural ambush-an agenda item introduced late, a confrontation that feels unpredictable-can leave him cold with anger. He experiences these moments less as annoyance than as a bodily alarm. His jaw tightens, his thoughts narrow, and afterward he cannot remember parts of what others said. He goes home exhausted from appearing calm.

He speaks most painfully about the guilt. He knows, rationally, that he did what he could that day. He has been told this by fellow soldiers, by his wife, by his own mind in its more reasonable hours. But another part of him returns to small details endlessly: where he was sitting, how quickly he moved, whether he should have noticed something earlier on the road. He does not say he believes he should have died; rather, he carries a quieter, more corrosive thought-that he continued into a full life of elections, anniversaries, and ordinary complaints while others did not.

Now, nearly three decades later, he presents as successful, articulate, and disciplined. He still attends council sessions, shakes hands, and speaks confidently about zoning and transport. Yet he lives as if catastrophe is always just offstage. The war does not feel past to him in the way it seems to others. It arrives in fragments-in dreams, in sound, in flashes of anger, in the way he patrols his own house before dawn-and each time he is pulled back into a state of readiness he cannot fully turn off.
